Teach me the essential JavaScript array methods: map, filter, reduce, find, some, every, flatMap and slice, with one combined example.

```js
const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Laptop', price: 1200, inStock: true },
  { id: 2, name: 'Mouse', price: 25, inStock: true },
  { id: 3, name: 'Keyboard', price: 75, inStock: false },
  { id: 4, name: 'Monitor', price: 300, inStock: true }
];

const names = products.map(p => p.name);              // transform
const cheap = products.filter(p => p.price < 100);    // select
const total = products
  .filter(p => p.inStock)
  .reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0);              // accumulate -> 1525
const mouse = products.find(p => p.id === 2);         // first match or undefined
const anyExpensive = products.some(p => p.price > 1000); // true
const allPriced = products.every(p => p.price > 0);   // true
const tags = products.flatMap(p => [p.name[0], p.id]); // map + flatten one level
const top2 = products.slice(0, 2);                    // shallow copy of a section

console.log(names, total, mouse.name, top2.length);
```
Guidelines: `map` returns a new array of the same length; `filter` and `slice` return new arrays and never mutate; `reduce` folds the array into any value; `find`/`some`/`every` short-circuit. Avoid `forEach` when you need a result, and remember `map`/`filter`/`reduce` never mutate the original array.

Debug: My flexbox container is not centering its items even though I wrote display:flex. What am I doing wrong?

**Symptom:** `display: flex` is set, but items hug the top-left corner or only center on one axis. **Diagnosis:** flex centering needs BOTH axis properties, and several things silently defeat it: ```html
Center me
``` ```css /* BROKEN: no height — a block div is content-sized, so there is no vertical space to center within */ .wrap { display: flex; align-items: center; } /* FIXED: give the container a size and set BOTH axes */ .wrap { display: flex; justify-content: center; /* main axis (horizontal in the default row) */ align-items: center; /* cross axis (vertical) */ height: 100vh; /* or 100% of a sized parent */ } ``` Other silent killers — check in DevTools: - A typo like `display: flexbox` or the rule overridden by a stronger selector (shown struck-through in the Styles panel). - The child has `position: absolute`, which removes it from flex flow — center it relative to its positioned parent instead. - `flex-direction: column` swaps the axes: `justify-content` becomes vertical. - The container itself has collapsed width (e.g., it is an inline element or an unsized flex item). **Fix:** confirm the computed style really shows `display: flex`, set both `justify-content` and `align-items`, and make sure the container actually has height/width to center within. **Prevention:** keep the one-liner `display: flex; place-items: center;` (shorthand for both axes) together with an explicit size on the container; for centering a single child, `margin: auto` on the child inside a flex container also works.

Debug: I positioned a badge with position:absolute and top/right, but it anchors to the page corner instead of the card it is inside. Why?

**Symptom:** an absolutely-positioned element ignores its visual parent and snaps to the corner of the page or of some distant ancestor. **Root cause:** `position: absolute` positions against the nearest ancestor whose position is NOT `static` — not necessarily the DOM parent. If the card is `position: static` (the default), the badge climbs the tree until it finds a positioned ancestor, often ``. ```html
3
``` ```css /* BROKEN */ .badge { position: absolute; top: -8px; right: -8px; } /* FIXED: make the intended parent the containing block */ .card { position: relative; } .badge { position: absolute; top: -8px; right: -8px; } ``` Any of these on an ancestor ALSO creates the containing block: `absolute`, `fixed`, `sticky`, plus `transform`, `filter`, `will-change` or `contain: layout`. **Diagnosis:** in DevTools, select the badge, then temporarily give suspicious ancestors `outline: 1px solid red` while nudging `top/right` — you will see which box it actually measures against. The Computed panel shows each ancestor's `position`. **Fix:** add `position: relative` to the intended parent (it changes nothing else visually). **Prevention:** pair every `position: absolute` child with an explicit `position: relative` on its wrapper as a habit, and remember `transform`/`filter` also capture absolute children — check ancestors before blaming the CSS.

Debug: My dropdown has z-index: 9999 but it still renders UNDER another element. Why does z-index not work?

**Symptom:** a huge `z-index` loses to a smaller one, or z-index seems ignored completely.

**Root causes — z-index only applies to positioned/flex/grid items, and only within its stacking context:**

1. **No position:** z-index is ignored on static elements.
```css
.dropdown { z-index: 9999; }                     /* ignored: static */
.dropdown { position: absolute; z-index: 9999; } /* now it applies */
```
2. **Trapped in a stacking context:** if a parent creates one (`position` + `z-index`, `opacity < 1`, `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, `isolation`, `mix-blend-mode`), the dropdown's 9999 competes only INSIDE that parent. If the parent's own context sits below the rival, no child z-index can escape.
```css
.modal-wrap { position: absolute; opacity: 0.99; z-index: 1; } /* context A */
.sidebar    { position: relative; z-index: 10; }               /* context B beats ALL of A */
```

**Diagnosis:** in DevTools walk up the tree in the Elements panel checking Computed styles of each ancestor for `transform`, `opacity`, `filter`, `will-change`, `position/z-index` — the first ancestor creating a stacking context is the ceiling your element cannot rise above.

**Fix:** raise the z-index of the correct ANCESTOR (the stacking-context owner), or remove the accidental context-creating property (drop `opacity: 0.99`, delete an unused `transform`), or scope layers deliberately with `isolation: isolate`.

**Prevention:** keep a small z-index scale (10/20/30) instead of 9999 arms races; know which properties create stacking contexts before layering components; wrap self-contained widgets in `isolation: isolate` so their internals never leak out.
